entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ala-ad-din Tarmashirin Khan, who reigned from approximately 1326 to 1334, was a pivotal figure in the tumultuous history of the Chagatai Khanate, a successor state to the Mongol Empire. His rule marked a significant turning point, primarily due to his conversion to Islam and his efforts to centralize power and assert the khanate's independence against both the Ilkhanate to the west and the Yuan Dynasty to the east. Tarmashirin's reign is characterized by both military success and deep internal divisions, reflecting the complex ethnic and religious tapestry of Central Asia in the early 14th century. His policies and personal choices directly contributed to the khanate's eventual fragmentation, shaping the geopolitical landscape of the Silk Road for centuries.

Tarmashirin ascended to the throne following the brief and unstable reign of Duwa Timur, consolidating his position through a series of military campaigns. A defining moment of his rule was his formal conversion to Islam, adopting the name Ala-ad-din, which alienated the traditionalist Mongol aristocracy who adhered to Tengrism and resented the perceived shift away from nomadic customs. Despite this internal discord, Tarmashirin launched successful military expeditions, notably a major invasion of India in 1327-1328, reaching as far as Delhi and extracting a substantial tribute from the Delhi Sultanate. He also engaged in diplomatic and military skirmishes with the Yuan Dynasty, challenging their suzerainty over the eastern parts of the Chagatai territories.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Tarmashirin's conversion to Islam and subsequent policies significantly altered the religious and political landscape of the Chagatai Khanate, contributing to its internal divisions and external conflicts. His reign marked a pivotal moment in the khanate's trajectory towards irreversible fragmentation into distinct eastern and western entities.
